guides.title: Species 8472
guides.summary: Species 8472 is a tripedal species from fluidic space, known for its organic bioships, its total immunity to Borg assimilation, and the devastating war it fought against the Borg Collective in the Delta Quadrant.

sections.heading: Fluidic Space: The Realm Beyond the Galaxy
sections.body:
Species 8472 does not originate anywhere in the known galaxy. Its home is fluidic space, a self-contained dimensional realm in which every point is suffused with a dense organic fluid rather than vacuum. Stars, planets and dust are absent; the realm itself appears to be at least partly biological in character, and the species moves through it as naturally as starships move through space. Access between fluidic space and normal space is achieved through quantum singularities, apertures the species can open and close at will from aboard its vessels.

The designation itself is not the species' own. It is the catalogue number assigned by the Borg Collective, which numbers every species it encounters in order of first contact. No record exists of what the beings call themselves, and no formal name has been adopted by Federation xenologists. Because almost every early report of the species came through Borg data or through USS Voyager's encounters, the Borg designation has remained the standard reference throughout Starfleet records.

sections.heading: Physiology of a Formidable Species
sections.body:
Members of Species 8472 stand roughly three metres tall and walk on three legs, a tripedal arrangement that gives them startling speed and stability. Their bodies are extraordinarily dense with genetic information: scans record a genome many times more complex than that of any known humanoid species, arranged in a multi-stranded structure unlike the double helix common to most Alpha Quadrant life. This density underlies an immune response of unmatched aggression. Foreign cells, implants and microscopic machines introduced into their tissue are attacked and destroyed almost immediately, which is why standard Borg assimilation nanoprobes fail against them entirely.

The species is telepathic. Individuals communicate with one another mind to mind, and their vessels respond to thought rather than to consoles. Contact with outside minds is possible for particularly sensitive telepaths; the Ocampa Kes was able to receive their communications during Voyager's first encounters. Their cells are also dangerous in themselves — tissue from the species can infect and consume humanoid flesh, a property that made even a wounded specimen a hazard to boarding parties.

sections.heading: Bioships and Organic Technology
sections.body:
Everything Species 8472 builds is grown. Its vessels, universally described as bioships, are living organisms composed of the same cellular material as their pilots, and the pilot interfaces with the ship neurally, directing it as an extension of the body. Bioships are small by capital-ship standards but overwhelmingly armed. Their primary weapon is a focused energy discharge capable of cutting through Borg cube hulls in seconds, and their organic hulls shrug off weapons fire that would cripple a conventional vessel.

The most feared application of the technology is a combined firing configuration. Groups of bioships — eight escorts channelling energy through a ninth — can merge their discharges into a single beam of planet-destroying magnitude. Borg records document entire assimilated worlds annihilated this way during the war in the Delta Quadrant. Because the ships are alive, they heal rather than undergo repair, and they travel between fluidic space and normal space through quantum singularities generated on demand. Federation engineering analysis of the technology remains almost entirely theoretical; no intact bioship has ever been recovered.

sections.heading: The War Against the Borg
sections.body:
The war began with a Borg miscalculation. In 2373 the Collective opened apertures into fluidic space, judging that a realm of purely biological life offered raw material for assimilation and a step toward its ideal of perfection. It found instead the single most assimilation-resistant species on record. Nanoprobes died in 8472 tissue, boarding actions failed, and the Collective's numerical advantage meant nothing against bioship weaponry.

Species 8472 answered the invasion by carrying the war into the Delta Quadrant. Its ships destroyed Borg cubes by the hundreds and burned assimilated worlds outright, with Borg losses within months measured in the millions of drones. The telepathic declaration received during the campaign — that the weak would perish — suggested the species had concluded that all life in the galaxy shared the Borg's aggression, and had resolved on a purge rather than a defensive war. For a brief period the Collective, for the first time in its recorded history, faced an enemy it could neither assimilate nor outfight, and it was losing.

sections.heading: Voyager, the Nanoprobe Weapon, and an Uneasy Truce
sections.body:
USS Voyager entered the war's path in 2373 while crossing Borg territory. Its crew developed the one weapon that ever worked: Borg nanoprobes reprogrammed by Voyager's medical hologram to overcome the 8472 immune response. In exchange for safe passage, Voyager shared the design with the Collective — the alliance that brought aboard the drone later known as Seven of Nine. Warheads carrying the modified nanoprobes destroyed several bioships, and Species 8472 withdrew into fluidic space, ending the open war.

The final recorded contact came in 2375, when Voyager discovered a terrasphere: a full-scale recreation of Starfleet Academy and its San Francisco surroundings, populated by 8472 operatives genetically altered into convincing human form. The installation was rehearsing infiltration of Earth, apparently in expectation of a Federation invasion of fluidic space. Voyager's officers instead opened negotiations, exchanged intelligence for goodwill, and secured an agreement to stand down. No hostile contact has been recorded since, though the species' capabilities are unchanged and its long-term intentions remain unknown.

guides.title: The Breen
guides.summary: The Breen are a secretive civilisation of the Breen Confederacy, known only through their refrigeration suits, snouted helmets and unintelligible vocoder speech; long a race of raiders and slavers, the Breen joined the Dominion in 2375 and struck Earth itself.

sections.heading: The Hidden People
sections.body:
No outsider has a verified account of what a Breen looks like. Every Breen ever recorded in contact with another species has appeared in a full-body environmental suit topped by a distinctive snouted helmet, and every Breen voice ever heard has come through a vocoder as a burst of harsh electronic garble — a signal their own equipment renders into meaning for them, and which universal translators handle inconsistently for anyone else. Even the Breen's wartime allies were granted no exception: senior Dominion and Cardassian officers who served beside Breen commanders for months never saw a face, and the Breen offered none.

The concealment is total enough that basic facts about the species remain open questions — their number of sexes, their diet, their lifespan, even whether every suited figure is the same species at all. Around this void, other powers have grown proverbs. The Romulans, who admire caution, say one should never turn one's back on a Breen. Others note that in two centuries of contact, the Breen have never once been caught explaining themselves. Whatever the Breen are, they have made ignorance of it a matter of state policy, and enforced it perfectly.

sections.heading: The Homeworld Question
sections.body:
For most of two centuries the settled assumption was that the Breen homeworld is a frozen waste, and that the refrigeration suits exist to carry that cold with them — the species' popular epithet in several languages amounts to the icemen. The assumption fit the suits, fit the Confederacy's remoteness, and fit the general air of chill the Breen cultivate.

It may be wrong. Senior Dominion officials who visited Breen during the alliance of 2375 described the homeworld as temperate — by one account, quite comfortable. If that report is accurate, the suits are not an environmental necessity at all, and their purpose becomes a matter of speculation: cultural armour, a security doctrine made wearable, or a physiological need unrelated to temperature. Records differ, and a third possibility is taken seriously by intelligence analysts: that the contradiction is deliberate, and the Breen seed disinformation about themselves as routinely as other powers issue press statements. A related legend holds that the Breen have no blood; no autopsy available to Federation medicine has ever confirmed or denied it, which is of course exactly how the Breen would prefer every question about them to end.

sections.heading: Raiders and Slavers
sections.body:
Before the Dominion War the Breen Confederacy held no formal quarrel with any major power, and needed none: its subjects made their living at the quadrant's expense anyway. Breen privateers raided shipping along half a dozen borders, striking fast, taking cargo and crews, and vanishing toward space no fleet cared to follow them into. Breen mercenaries and bounty hunters hired out to whoever paid, valued for their weapons technology and their perfect indifference to the politics of the job. And the Breen took slaves — not as commerce in the Orion manner, but as labour for their own industries.

The best-documented case is Dozaria: when a Cardassian vessel carrying Bajoran prisoners crashed on that desert world in the 2360s, the survivors of both species were captured by the Breen and worked for years in dilithium mines, their existence unknown until a rescue expedition reached the crash site long after. Confronted with such incidents, the Confederacy's response has been unvarying — no acknowledgement, no denial, no explanation. Punitive expeditions into Breen space have historically fared badly enough that most powers wrote the raids off as a cost of the frontier, which is precisely what the Breen appear to have counted on.

sections.heading: The Dominion Alliance and the Raid on Earth
sections.body:
In 2375, with the Dominion War grinding against them, the Dominion achieved a diplomatic stroke no one had predicted: the Breen Confederacy abandoned its long detachment and entered the war as a full Dominion ally. The price of Breen entry was kept secret even from the Dominion's existing Cardassian partners, and was widely rumoured to include territorial concessions carved from Cardassian space — a rumour that did measurable damage to Cardassian loyalty in the war's final months. Breen thermal-suited soldiers and Breen warships appeared on Dominion lines within weeks, commanded by officers with the rank-title Thot.

The alliance announced itself with a blow aimed at morale rather than strategy: a Breen strike force penetrated the Sol system and attacked Starfleet Headquarters on Earth, leaving the grounds burning beneath a shattered skyline. The raid's military value was modest — the force was destroyed, the damage repaired — but its meaning was not. Earth had not been struck by an enemy fleet in a generation, and the deepest core of Federation space had proved reachable by a power that, weeks earlier, most citizens could not have described beyond a helmet. The Breen had entered the war as they do everything: without warning, and to effect.

sections.heading: The Energy-Dampening Weapon and the War's End
sections.body:
The Breen brought the Dominion more than fleets: they brought a weapon nobody could answer. Breen warships mounted an energy-dissipating device that, on striking a target, drained its systems wholesale — propulsion, shields, weapons and power collapsing together, leaving a functioning crew inside an inert hull. At the Second Battle of Chin'toka the weapon was unveiled at scale, and an allied Federation-Klingon-Romulan fleet was annihilated; ships that had fought the Dominion for years died without landing an effective blow, and the allies briefly faced the prospect of losing the war to a single device.

The reprieve came from an engineering accident of Klingon design: one Klingon vessel survived the weapon, and analysis of why allowed Klingon ships — their systems adapted first — to hold the line alone while a general countermeasure was developed and distributed. Within months the weapon was neutralised across all three allied fleets, and the Breen advantage evaporated. When the Dominion surrendered at the end of 2375, Breen representatives stood among the signatories to the instruments ending the war, and then did what the Breen have always done: withdrew behind their borders, resumed their silence, and left every question about them exactly where they wanted it — unanswered.

guides.title: The El-Aurians
guides.summary: The El-Aurians are a long-lived species of listeners scattered across the galaxy after the Borg destroyed their homeworld; notable El-Aurians include Guinan of the Enterprise-D and the scientist Tolian Soran.

sections.heading: A Species of Listeners
sections.body:
The El-Aurians describe themselves, when they describe themselves at all, as a race of listeners. The phrase is not a pleasantry. El-Aurians possess an unusual sensitivity to the people around them — an ability to attend to another being so completely that the speaker often resolves their own difficulty simply by being heard. Among many species this made El-Aurians sought after as advisors, hosts and confidants, and, less reputably, as manipulators; the talent serves a confidence artist as well as it serves a counsellor.

Outwardly El-Aurians are indistinguishable from humans, and they have moved quietly through human history without attracting notice. Their lifespans, however, are measured in centuries at minimum. Individuals born in the nineteenth century by Earth reckoning were still in evident good health in the late twenty-fourth, and no record establishes an upper limit. They age slowly, if at all, across the spans other species can observe. Combined with their habit of travel, this longevity means an El-Aurian's personal memory can span eras that other cultures know only as history.

sections.heading: The Destruction of the Homeworld
sections.body:
In the mid-twenty-third century the Borg Collective located and assimilated the El-Aurian homeworld. The attack was total: the planet's population was absorbed or destroyed, its cities levelled, and a civilisation that had endured for millennia ended in a matter of days. Only scattered survivors escaped — those off-world at the time, and those who fled aboard whatever vessels could outrun the cubes.

The El-Aurians thus became a diaspora people a generation before the Federation had even heard the word Borg. Survivors dispersed across the Alpha and Beta Quadrants and beyond, settling as individuals rather than colonies; no El-Aurian successor state was ever founded, and most survivors seem to have deliberately avoided gathering in numbers. Federation analysts note that El-Aurian warnings about the Borg circulated decades before the Collective's first incursion into Federation space in 2366, but were largely received as travellers' tales. Those who lived through the fall rarely speak of it in detail, and much of what Starfleet knows was assembled from fragments offered reluctantly, long after the fact.

sections.heading: The Lakul Disaster and the Nexus
sections.body:
In 2293 two transport ships, the SS Lakul and the SS Robert Fox, were carrying El-Aurian refugees to Earth when both were caught in the Nexus — a ribbon of temporal energy that crosses the galaxy on a recurring track. The ribbon's gravimetric distortions destroyed the Robert Fox with all aboard and were tearing the Lakul apart when the newly launched USS Enterprise-B, on its maiden voyage, answered the distress call. Forty-seven El-Aurians were beamed out of the Lakul before it broke up. The rescue cost the life of Captain James T. Kirk, recorded lost when the ribbon struck the Enterprise-B's hull — though later events at Veridian III would show that record to be incomplete.

The survivors carried a peculiar injury. Inside the Nexus a being experiences a state of pure, timeless contentment, and those pulled out of it did not all recover from its loss. Most rebuilt their lives and made their peace with ordinary time. At least one, the scientist Tolian Soran, spent the next eight decades attempting to re-enter the ribbon at any cost.

sections.heading: Guinan, Soran, and Other Notable El-Aurians
sections.body:
The best-documented El-Aurian in Starfleet records is Guinan, who served aboard the USS Enterprise-D as host of its Ten Forward lounge through much of the 2360s. Several centuries old, she had visited Earth as early as 1893, and Captain Jean-Luc Picard described their relationship as going beyond friendship and beyond family. Her counsel proved decisive more than once, most famously when she persuaded a Picard from an altered timeline that history itself had gone wrong and had to be put back.

Tolian Soran stands as her dark counterpart. A survivor of both the Borg and the Lakul, he destroyed entire stars to bend the Nexus ribbon's course toward a world where he could step back inside — culminating in 2371 at Veridian III, where collapsing the system's sun would have extinguished a pre-industrial civilisation on a neighbouring world. He was stopped by Picard and by James Kirk, drawn out of the Nexus for one final act. Other El-Aurians on record include Martus Mazur, an itinerant confidence artist: evidence that the listeners' gift carries no guarantee of virtue.

sections.heading: Perception Beyond the Ordinary
sections.body:
El-Aurian perception extends beyond attentive listening into territory that resists analysis. Guinan demonstrated an awareness of changes to the timeline itself: when an anomaly rewrote history around the Enterprise-D, she alone sensed that the ship's reality was wrong, without instruments and without explanation. El-Aurians pulled from the Nexus likewise retained an echo of themselves within it, a lingering connection to the ribbon that ordinary humanoids do not report.

The species also has some unexplained history with the Q Continuum. Guinan and the entity Q knew one another on sight and plainly distrusted one another, and Q described her people as a species not to be provoked — a remarkable statement from a being of effectively unlimited power. Whether these abilities are innate to all El-Aurians or cultivated by some is unrecorded; the species does not explain itself, and the handful of El-Aurians known to Starfleet have been consistent only in their discretion. Analysts note the pattern with interest and file it, as the El-Aurians themselves might suggest, under questions that answer themselves in time.

guides.title: The Gorn
guides.summary: The Gorn are a powerful reptilian species governed by the Gorn Hegemony, fiercely territorial and long hostile to outsiders; early Gorn encounters were violent, and formal contact began with the Cestus III incident of 2267.

sections.heading: Physiology
sections.body:
The Gorn are large reptilian bipeds, typically standing well over two metres, with thick scaled hide, clawed hands and immense physical strength. A mature Gorn can shatter rock and bend structural alloy bare-handed, shrug off phaser stun settings that would fell most humanoids, and continue fighting through injuries that would be immediately disabling in a mammalian species. Their hide provides substantial protection against blades, projectiles and environmental extremes, and they favour hot, arid conditions consistent with a cold-blooded metabolism.

Records of Gorn speed conflict. The adult encountered at Cestus III in 2267 moved slowly and deliberately, relying on endurance and power rather than agility, while earlier survivor accounts describe Gorn — particularly younger ones — as horrifyingly fast. Federation xenobiologists generally reconcile the two by life stage: the species appears to pass through distinct forms, with juveniles built for pursuit and slaughter and elders built for dominance and durability. Sensory descriptions also vary between accounts, from multifaceted compound eyes to slit-pupiled hunters' vision. Until the Hegemony permits systematic study — and it never has — the physiology of the Gorn remains assembled from battlefield observation rather than science.

sections.heading: Early Encounters and Restricted Records
sections.body:
Decades before the Federation formally recognised the Gorn as a governed civilisation, vessels and colonies along the unclaimed border regions were meeting them in the worst possible way. Accounts from the 2230s through the 2250s describe ships found drifting with their crews gone, colonies silenced without a distress call completed, and a small number of survivors whose testimony was so grim that Starfleet restricted it. Those survivors spoke of capture rather than mere attack — of the Gorn taking the living for purposes that only later became understood.

The classification of these records had a lasting consequence: a generation of Starfleet officers served without knowing what the Gorn were, and command-level briefings treated the species as rumour. When the attack on Cestus III came in 2267, the officers responding believed they were facing an unknown power, and contemporary logs describe it as a first contact. Later historians, with the archives opened, treat 2267 not as the first meeting but as the first meeting the Federation was permitted to remember. Records differ on how many earlier incidents were Gorn action and how many were attributed to them after the fact.

sections.heading: Breeding and the Hatchling Threat
sections.body:
The most feared aspect of Gorn biology is how they reproduce. Survivor accounts and recovered medical records agree on the essentials: Gorn implant eggs in living hosts of other species, and the young erupt from the host on hatching, killing it. A single implantation can yield several hatchlings, and the newborns' first act is often to fight one another until a dominant survivor emerges. That survivor grows with extraordinary speed, hunting from its first hours, and juveniles that encounter prey together display coordinated pack behaviour that no newborn animal should be capable of.

Why a starfaring, tool-using civilisation retains so brutal a reproductive strategy is unknown. Some analysts argue the Hegemony deliberately preserves it as a weapon and a winnowing rite, selecting for the aggression the culture prizes; others suggest the Gorn simply do not regard other species as persons in any sense that would make the practice monstrous to them. What is certain is that the practice shaped every early encounter: vessels boarded by Gorn were not being raided for cargo. Standing Starfleet medical protocol treats any survivor of Gorn capture as a possible host until proven otherwise.

sections.heading: The Cestus III Incident
sections.body:
In 2267 the Federation outpost and colony on Cestus III was destroyed by an unidentified attacker, with heavy loss of life. A Federation starship responding to a falsified invitation was ambushed in orbit, and the attacking vessel fled toward unexplored space with the starship in pursuit. The attackers were Gorn — and from the Hegemony's perspective, the engagement was not aggression but defence. Cestus III lay within space the Gorn regarded as theirs, and the colony, established in good faith by a Federation that did not know the Hegemony existed, read to them as an invasion.

The pursuit ended when a vastly powerful third species, the Metrons, intervened. Objecting to violence in their region, they seized the two commanders and set them against each other in single combat on a prepared world, the loser's ship to be destroyed. The human captain, improvising a weapon from raw materials, defeated his Gorn counterpart — and then refused to kill him. The Metrons, who had expected savagery, released both ships. The refusal mattered: it converted a war-opening massacre into a negotiable border dispute, and the first real diplomacy between the Federation and the Hegemony followed from it.

sections.heading: The Hegemony and Later Relations
sections.body:
The Gorn state is known as the Gorn Hegemony, and its outward behaviour is consistent across two centuries of records: it marks its territory, defends it without warning or proportion, and otherwise wants little to do with anyone. The Hegemony rarely explains itself, does not host observers, and conducts what diplomacy it accepts through terse, formal exchanges. Analysts believe its internal politics reward dominance in roughly the way its hatchling broods do, but this is inference; no outsider has documented Gorn government from the inside.

After Cestus III, relations settled into a cold correctness. The border was clarified, the colony's destruction was folded into the settlement rather than avenged, and in time Cestus III itself was resettled — by the late twenty-fourth century it was a thriving Federation world, its history with the Gorn a chapter in its museums rather than a live wound. Individual Gorn have occasionally been recorded far from home as traders, enforcers or curiosities, but the species as a whole remains behind its own borders. The standing Starfleet assessment is unchanged for a century: the Gorn seek no conquest beyond their claim, and will accept no intrusion within it.

guides.title: The Jem'Hadar
guides.summary: The Jem'Hadar are the genetically engineered shock troops of the Dominion: soldiers grown rather than born, mature within days, bound to their Vorta overseers by the drug ketracel-white, and raised on a single creed — victory is life.

sections.heading: Engineered for War
sections.body:
The Jem'Hadar are not a species that evolved; they are a weapon that was designed. Created by the genetic engineers of the Dominion to serve as its army, Jem'Hadar are grown in birthing chambers rather than born, and their development is compressed to a degree no natural biology approaches: a newly decanted Jem'Hadar reaches full fighting maturity in roughly three days, emerging with language, combat instinct and an unconditional loyalty to the Dominion already in place. There is no Jem'Hadar childhood, no Jem'Hadar family, and no recorded Jem'Hadar female; reproduction is entirely a matter of the hatcheries.

Their design strips away every need that might distract a soldier. Jem'Hadar do not eat — their sole nourishment is delivered chemically — they require minimal rest, and they regard recreation, comfort and personal possession as concepts belonging to lesser beings. A Jem'Hadar soldier is complete the moment he can hold a weapon, and he will typically die holding one: the engineered lifespan is short, few Jem'Hadar live past fifteen years, and one who reaches twenty is accorded the rare title of Honoured Elder. Among Jem'Hadar this brevity is not regretted. A long life, in their creed, is merely evidence of too few battles.

sections.heading: Ketracel-White
sections.body:
The leash on the Dominion's army is a drug. Every Jem'Hadar is engineered with a built-in dependency on ketracel-white — an isogenic enzyme compound, called simply the white — which supplies all nourishment their bodies need and without which their own biochemistry turns on them. Deprivation follows a known and terrible course: discipline decays, then control, then sanity, and death follows in days. The Founders did not leave obedience to training; they wrote it into the bloodstream.

Distribution of the white is the exclusive office of the Vorta, the Dominion's administrators, and it is deliberately ritualised. Before an engagement the Vorta overseer dispenses each soldier's vial in a formal exchange of pledges, the unit's First accepting on behalf of his men; the ceremony restates, daily, who provides life and who owes service. Supply of the white is therefore the Dominion's true strategic vulnerability, and during the war in the Alpha Quadrant — cut off from the Gamma Quadrant's production — its depots and freighters were priority targets. Records note at least one Jem'Hadar born without the dependency, an anomaly the Dominion regarded as a defect. The Jem'Hadar themselves rarely resent the leash. To most of them, the white is simply what they are.

sections.heading: Doctrine and Belief
sections.body:
Jem'Hadar belief is brief enough to fit on a blade. The Founders — the shapeshifting rulers of the Dominion — are gods, their will is transmitted through the Vorta, and the purpose of a Jem'Hadar life is victory in their service. This is not metaphor to the Jem'Hadar; soldiers who have seen a Founder in person describe the experience in openly religious terms, and units have destroyed themselves without hesitation rather than allow harm to reach one. Whether the Founders deserve worship does not arise in Jem'Hadar thinking. That question is above his rank, and every Jem'Hadar knows his rank.

The creed's core is the phrase spoken before battle: victory is life. The full pre-battle recitation declares the soldiers already dead — they go into battle to reclaim their lives, and the dead need fear nothing. The formula is engineered psychology as much as liturgy: an army that considers itself dead cannot be broken by casualties, and no recorded Jem'Hadar force has ever surrendered as a unit. Obedience is likewise total, expressed in their own maxim that it is the order of things. The rare individual Jem'Hadar who questioned the order of things has entered the record precisely because he was rare.

sections.heading: Capabilities and Command
sections.body:
As individual soldiers the Jem'Hadar are among the most formidable humanoid combatants ever engineered. They possess great strength and resilience, tolerate injuries that would incapacitate most species, and carry an engineered ability called the shroud — a personal concealment that renders a Jem'Hadar effectively invisible to eye and sensor alike until he chooses to strike, or until deprivation of the white erodes the discipline the shroud requires. Their standard sidearm fires plasma charges laced with an anticoagulant designed to keep wounds killing after the battle passes, and their attack ships have been used as ramming weapons when commanders judged the trade worthwhile.

Command within a unit follows a numbered hierarchy: the First commands, the Second stands ready to replace him, and so on down the file. Rank is conferred by the Vorta overseer and can be revoked by him, but battlefield succession is automatic — kill a First and the Second simply becomes First, which makes decapitation tactics nearly useless against Jem'Hadar formations. Late in the Dominion War a distinction emerged between the original Gamma Quadrant stock and Alphas, Jem'Hadar bred in the Alpha Quadrant and optimised for its conditions; the two lines regarded each other with a rivalry the Dominion found useful and kept carefully short of open feud.

sections.heading: Service History
sections.body:
The Alpha Quadrant learned what the Jem'Hadar were in 2370, in the Dominion's first deliberate demonstration. Jem'Hadar forces overran Federation and civilian positions in the Gamma Quadrant, held boarding parties at bay with contemptuous ease, and — when a Galaxy-class starship withdrew from an engagement — destroyed it with a suicide ramming attack their own commanders described as instruction: the Dominion wished it understood that retreat would not be punished with pursuit, but with annihilation. The lesson was received. Every subsequent Federation contact with the Dominion was shaped by the knowledge of what its army would do.

Through the Dominion War of 2373 to 2375 the Jem'Hadar were the backbone of Dominion power on every front — the infantry of the occupations, the crews of the attack wings, the garrisons of the conquered systems. They fought at Chin'toka, on Cardassia, and in every engagement between, with a consistency their enemies came to rely upon tactically: Jem'Hadar do not rout, do not loot, and do not disobey. When the Founders ordered the war ended, the army that had never surrendered stood down in a day — the final proof of what the Jem'Hadar had always said of themselves. They were not conquerors. They were the will of the Founders, given form and a rifle.

guides.title: The Orion Syndicate and the Orions
guides.summary: The Orions are a green-skinned humanoid civilisation professing neutrality, while the Orion Syndicate — a criminal network of smugglers, pirates, slavers and extortionists — operates across the quadrant; Orion women and Orion men both figure in its trade, not always in the roles outsiders assume.

sections.heading: The Orions
sections.body:
The Orions are a humanoid species distinguished by green skin, physical vigour and one of the oldest continuous merchant cultures in known space. Orion vessels were trading — and raiding — along the spacelanes long before United Earth reached warp, and Orion commercial colonies, free ports and clan compounds can be found scattered across the quadrant far beyond any formal Orion border. Orion society is organised around trading clans and family combines rather than a strong central state, and its public face has always been the market: anything can be bought in an Orion port, and the price is the only morality reliably enforced.

Officially, Orion policy is neutrality. The Orion government has declared itself neutral in every major interstellar conflict of the last two centuries, taking no side between the Federation, the Klingon Empire, the Romulans or any other power. The declaration is real as far as it goes — Orion fleets do not march — but it has always been a merchant's neutrality: a refusal to close the shop to any customer. Weapons, information and contraband have flowed through Orion hands to every belligerent of every war, and the clans have prospered from conflicts they took no formal part in.

sections.heading: The Slave Markets and the Pheromone Deception
sections.body:
The Orion institution most notorious among outsiders is the slave trade, and above all the sale of Orion women — advertised across two centuries of black markets as prized, docile property. The trade is real, and many of its victims, of many species, are exactly what they appear to be: captives sold for labour and worse. But the most famous commodity of the markets conceals the trade's strangest fact.

In 2154 an incident aboard an Earth starship revealed it. Three Orion women, presented as escaped slaves, progressively took command of the vessel's crew without lifting a hand: Orion women produce pheromones of extraordinary potency, heightening suggestibility and aggression in males of many species, sickening some others, and leaving the women's chosen instruments convinced their obedience was their own idea. The supposed merchandise had been directing the supposed merchants throughout. How widely this inversion runs through Orion society is genuinely unclear — records differ, and Orion clans profit from every rumour about themselves — but Federation analysts have treated one lesson as settled since: in any Orion arrangement, assume the party who appears to hold the power may not be the one who does.

sections.heading: The Syndicate
sections.body:
The Orion Syndicate is the organised criminal enterprise most consistently associated with Orion space, though its membership has never been limited to Orions. Its business is everything law prohibits and demand sustains: smuggling, piracy, slave trading, extortion, counterfeiting, gambling, forgery of identities and manifests, and contract killing. It is structured less like a gang than like a merchant combine gone feral — bosses, brokers and soldiers bound by shares, debts and fear.

Membership is bought, not merely joined: a candidate pays in, is vouched for, and is thereafter owned. The Syndicate's discipline is its most feared feature. Members who steal from it, inform on it or simply fail it are killed, and the organisation's reach into police services, courts and protective custody is such that witnesses against it very rarely live to testify. Entire prosecutions have collapsed on the eve of trial with the death of every cooperating witness. This enforcement record, advertised by the Syndicate itself, does much of its work for it: on many frontier worlds, no threat needs to be spoken beyond the observation that the Syndicate knows a name.

sections.heading: Reach and Method
sections.body:
The Syndicate's genius is usefulness. It does not seek territory or ideology; it seeks position — a share in a shipping combine here, a debt held over a magistrate there, a protection arrangement covering a mining settlement that the local authorities cannot defend. On worlds along the frontiers it often functions as a shadow government, taxing commerce through protection fees and settling disputes its own way, tolerated because it is orderly and feared because of why it is orderly.

Its trade in information may exceed its trade in goods. Syndicate brokers buy and sell intelligence to all comers, and during the Dominion War years its contacts were found running errands for Dominion intelligence — arranging meetings, laundering identities, and brokering an attempted operation against Klingon leadership — while other branches sold services to the Dominion's enemies. Starfleet Intelligence has run repeated penetration operations against the Syndicate, at least one of which, in the 2370s, placed an officer inside a Syndicate cell for an extended period; the operations confirmed the organisation's structure and its Dominion contacts, and also the human cost of befriending men one has come to arrest. The Syndicate survived every such operation. It always has.

sections.heading: The Long Arc
sections.body:
The Syndicate's history tracks the quadrant's. In the twenty-third century its signature was piracy and provocation: Orion raiders preyed on shipping in contested regions, and in 2268 an Orion vessel attacked delegations travelling to the Babel conference — a suicide mission, its crew equipped to die rather than be identified, intended to wreck a diplomatic settlement from which neutral Orion traders in dilithium stood to lose. The affair, exposed aboard the Federation flagship, embarrassed the official Orion posture of neutrality without ever formally piercing it; the government deplored, denied and continued.

In the twenty-fourth century the Syndicate matured into the quadrant's underworld bank and broker, thriving in the disorder of the Dominion War. And in the deep future the pattern completed itself: by the thirty-second century, in the long chaos that followed the collapse of galactic dilithium supplies, Orion cartels no longer hid behind governments but stood as one — the Emerald Chain, an Orion-Andorian mercantile power that ruled worlds openly for a time. Records of that era lie far outside this archive's core period, but the arc is continuous and characteristically Orion: commerce first, law optional, and patience above all.

guides.title: The Tholians
guides.summary: The Tholians are a non-humanoid crystalline species of the Tholian Assembly, thriving in superheated environments lethal to humanoids and famed for punctuality, absolute territoriality, and the energy-web weapon known as the Tholian web.

sections.heading: Crystalline Physiology
sections.body:
The Tholians are among the most alien of the known spacefaring species: they are not humanoid, not mammalian, and not even conventionally organic. A Tholian body is a faceted crystalline form, described in twenty-second-century imaging as a hard, angular carapace with radially arranged lower limbs and a pair of grasping forelimbs, glowing from within with shifting light. They are native to environments of extraordinary heat — comfortable well above two hundred degrees Celsius under crushing pressure — and conditions that humanoids find pleasant are, to a Tholian, a lethal cold. An unprotected Tholian exposed to standard starship temperatures suffers cracking of the carapace within minutes and dies soon after.

Tholian communication is equally alien: a rapid, high-frequency chorus of chirps and harmonic shrieks that universal translators render only with difficulty. Some accounts suggest Tholians share thought among themselves in ways that go beyond sound — a lattice or communal awareness — but the Assembly has never confirmed how its people think, and records differ. What is well established is precision: Tholian speech, once translated, is exact, literal and unadorned, and Tholians treat ambiguity in others as somewhere between incompetence and insult.

sections.heading: The Assembly: Precision and Territory
sections.body:
The Tholian state is called the Tholian Assembly, and its reputation rests on two traits observed consistently for over two centuries: punctuality and territoriality. Tholian punctuality is a byword across the quadrant — an Assembly vessel that agrees to a rendezvous will arrive to the second, and expects the same of others; lateness has ended negotiations before they began. The trait appears to be not courtesy but worldview: a civilisation of crystal seems to regard time, order and boundary as aspects of one discipline.

Territorially, the Assembly annexes and enforces without apology. Regions it claims are announced, and intrusion is met with force regardless of the intruder's intent, size or flag; distress is not accepted as an excuse. Yet the same literal-mindedness makes the Assembly a reliable counterparty — agreements it signs are kept exactly as written, neither more nor less. Commerce with the Assembly is limited but real. Its most famous export is Tholian silk, a fabric of extraordinary fineness prized as a diplomatic gift and status good on many worlds; how a species of living crystal produces it is one of many questions the Assembly declines to answer.

sections.heading: The Tholian Web
sections.body:
The Assembly's signature weapon is the energy structure known simply as the Tholian web. Working in pairs or larger formations, Tholian vessels spin filaments of energy through space around a target, each pass laying another strand of a closing lattice. The process is unhurried and almost ceremonial; a target that watches long enough sees itself being sealed inside a glowing cage. When the web is complete it contracts, and a vessel enclosed within it is immobilised, crushed, or dragged wherever the web-spinners intend. The web's construction can be interrupted by destroying or driving off the spinning vessels, which is why Tholian doctrine favours engaging targets already damaged, outnumbered or diplomatically pinned.

The web is not only a weapon. Tholians have been observed using web structures for containment and salvage — fencing a hazard, holding a derelict, or sealing a region of unstable space. This dual use reflects the Tholian cast of mind: the web is less an armament than an instrument of enclosure, applied wherever the Assembly has decided that something must not move. Starfleet tactical doctrine since the twenty-third century has been blunt on the subject: a ship that cannot leave the area before a web closes should never allow one to be started.

sections.heading: Recorded Encounters
sections.body:
Earth's dealings with the Tholians began in the 2150s, and began strangely. In 2152 Tholian vessels intervened to seize a small craft displaced from centuries in the future — the earliest evidence that the Assembly took an active interest in temporal matters, and was willing to fight established powers to secure temporally displaced objects. Sporadic contact through that decade established the pattern that still holds: the Tholians appear suddenly, state their claim once, and act.

The most famous incident came in 2268, when the Federation starship Defiant was lost in a region of spatial interphase — a weakening between dimensional planes — near space claimed by the Assembly. A sister ship attempting rescue was attacked by Tholian vessels and partially enclosed in a web before escaping; the Defiant itself faded out of normal space entirely during the confrontation. Tholian records of the derelict's fate, if any exist, have never been shared, and Federation files on the loss remain incomplete. Encounters in the centuries since have been intermittent and cold — border incidents, terse exchanges, occasional narrow cooperation — with the Assembly neither ally nor enemy, but a fixed hazard on the charts.

sections.heading: The Temporal Question
sections.body:
A recurring thread runs through two centuries of Tholian contact: time. The Assembly's forces have repeatedly appeared wherever temporal displacement, interphasic instability or objects from other eras were involved, and always with the same aim — possession. The 2152 seizure of a future-built craft was pursued with a determination out of proportion to the object's apparent value, and the interphase region that claimed the Defiant in 2268 lay close against Tholian space, where Assembly vessels arrived with suspicious speed.

Why the Tholians care is unresolved. One school holds that their crystalline physiology is unusually sensitive to temporal and dimensional distortion, making such phenomena a matter of survival rather than curiosity; another that the Assembly conducts a deliberate, long-running programme of temporal technology acquisition, and was a quiet participant in the era of temporal conflicts that Federation records treat with heavy classification. The Assembly itself has never explained, confirmed or denied anything; inquiries on the subject are met with silence or with the standard notice that the region of the inquiry is claimed. Analysts are left with the observed rule: where time is broken, expect Tholians.

guides.title: The Vorta
guides.summary: The Vorta are the cloned administrators, diplomats and overseers of the Dominion: they speak for the Founders, whom they worship as gods, command the Jem'Hadar through control of ketracel-white, and return from death as numbered clones of themselves.

sections.heading: Origins: The Founders' Reward
sections.body:
The Vorta account of their own origin is a parable of gratitude. Ages ago, the story runs, the Vorta were small, timid, tree-dwelling creatures on a forest world — clever enough to hide, and nothing more. When a Changeling fleeing a mob of solids took refuge among them, a family of Vorta concealed it from its pursuers, and the grateful shapeshifter promised that one day the Vorta would be transformed and set above all other solids as part of a great empire. The Founders kept the promise: the Vorta were remade into the humanoid servants they are today, the administrators of the Dominion the Changelings built.

Whether any of this happened is another matter. The story exists solely in the telling of the Vorta and their gods, and even senior Vorta have conceded, in candid moments, that they have no way of knowing whether it is true — the Founders wrote the Vorta, and could as easily have written their memory of the debt. Records differ on nothing here, because there are no records; there is only the parable. Its function, true or not, is plain: a species that owes its very shape to its gods does not ask why it serves them.

sections.heading: Physiology by Design
sections.body:
The Vorta body is a curriculum of the Founders' priorities. Vorta are slight, pale humanoids with distinctive violet eyes and elongated ears, engineered for the work of administration rather than war. Their hearing is superb; their eyesight, by their own cheerful admission, is comparatively weak — a trade their creators evidently thought acceptable in a species meant to listen. They are immune to most known poisons, a precaution any negotiator dining at a hundred alien tables learns to appreciate, and they require little in the way of comfort. More curiously, the Founders left the Vorta with no sense of aesthetics: by their own account they cannot truly appreciate art, music or beauty, and individual Vorta have remarked on the omission with something between amusement and wistfulness.

One capability appears in the early record and then vanishes. The first Vorta encountered by the Federation, in 2370, demonstrated potent telekinesis — projected force employed as both demonstration and weapon. No Vorta observed since has shown any such ability, and records differ on the explanation: an engineered variant line, an ability later withdrawn, or a deception staged for first contact. With the Vorta, the last possibility can never be excluded; misdirection is not a flaw in their design but a feature of it.

sections.heading: Cloning and Succession
sections.body:
Vorta do not, in the ordinary sense, die. Each Vorta is a clone, one activation in a numbered series, and when a Vorta is killed — or terminated for cause — a new clone of the same line is activated with the memories of its predecessors transferred substantially intact. A Vorta introducing himself may note, in passing, that he is the fourth, fifth or eighth of his name, in the tone another being might use to mention a change of posting. Death, for a Vorta, is an administrative event; continuity of service is the point, and the Dominion's institutional memory walks around in cloned bodies.

The system has edges. Memory transfer is imperfect, and successive activations of one line can differ subtly in temperament — colleagues of long-serving lines have been known to compare activations as one compares vintages. Clones judged defective are terminated and replaced, a fate the Vorta discuss without apparent horror, and lines that fail the Founders too gravely are ended altogether: termination of the entire series is the Dominion's capital sentence for its administrators. The practical consequence for the Dominion's enemies is grim arithmetic. Killing a Vorta accomplishes almost nothing; within weeks, the same smile, slightly renumbered, resumes the same negotiation.

sections.heading: Role in the Dominion
sections.body:
The Vorta are the Dominion's entire civil service. They are its diplomats, its intelligence officers, its scientists and its colonial administrators; every function of the Dominion that is not fighting or ruling is, somewhere, a Vorta's desk. Their most visible office is command of the Jem'Hadar: each Jem'Hadar formation answers to a Vorta overseer, and the overseer's authority rests on the most reliable foundation the Founders could devise — exclusive control of ketracel-white, the drug without which the soldiers die. The daily dispensing ritual restates the arrangement: the Vorta provides life, the Jem'Hadar owe service, and the Founders own both.

The relationship between overseer and soldiers is functional rather than warm. Jem'Hadar privately despise most Vorta as soft, scheming and personally cowardly; the Vorta regard the Jem'Hadar as superb instruments requiring careful handling, and both views are, by design, correct. Vorta in the field carry one further piece of standard equipment: a termination implant, to be triggered upon capture. Suicide before interrogation is a duty owed to the Founders' secrets, and most Vorta speak of the implant with the mild pride of officials entrusted with sensitive files. Whether a given Vorta would actually use it has, on the record, varied with the Vorta.

sections.heading: Conduct in the War
sections.body:
During the Dominion's conflict with the Alpha Quadrant powers, the Vorta were its public face, and the face wore a smile. Vorta diplomatic style blends unfailing courtesy with unconcealed menace: reasonable terms offered in a pleasant voice, with the fleet behind them left to speak for itself. Federation negotiators learned to treat Vorta charm as an instrument — every kindness calculated, every concession pre-authorised, and every conversation reported to the Founders. Yet the war record also shows the Vorta were never mere mouthpieces. Individual lines displayed unmistakable individual character: one field supervisor coldly bargained away the lives of his own starving Jem'Hadar to save himself; another line's successive clones served through the entire political arc of the war, from first infiltration to the final surrender, scheming against rivals, flattering allies and, at the end, standing beside the last Founder in the ruins of the war he had helped conduct.

What never varied was the worship. Vorta loyalty to the Founders survived defeats, humiliations and in most cases even personal disillusionment; a Vorta who doubted his gods remained a Vorta who obeyed them. The Dominion's enemies found this the hardest thing about them to negotiate with. Terms, the Vorta would discuss endlessly. The faith was not on the table.

guides.title: Vulcans
guides.summary: A civilisation that chose discipline over extinction: Vulcan biology, the logic tradition, and what the choice cost.

sections.heading: Biology and Homeworld
sections.body: Vulcans evolved on a hot, arid, high-gravity world with a thin atmosphere, and nearly every physical trait follows from that. They are markedly stronger than humans and require less water and less sleep. Their hearing is acute, their eyes carry an inner lid against glare and dust, and their circulatory system is built around copper-bearing blood, which gives their blood a green cast and their complexions a faintly olive tone. Their internal organs are arranged differently enough from the human plan that a physician trained on one will do harm assuming the other — a detail the setting uses whenever it wants a medical crisis that competence alone cannot solve. They possess a degree of conscious control over their own physiology that humans do not: the ability to slow injury, to redirect blood flow away from a wound, and to enter a deep healing trance that suspends most bodily activity while damage is repaired. This is presented as trained rather than automatic, an application of the same discipline that governs their emotional life. Vulcans are also touch-telepaths. Contact permits a joining of minds — used for healing, for the transfer of memory, and in extremity for the preservation of a mind outside its body. The practice is treated as deeply intimate and is not undertaken casually, and its existence quietly explains a good deal about Vulcan reserve: a species that can genuinely enter another's mind has strong reasons to be formal about ordinary contact.

sections.heading: The Discipline of Logic
sections.body: The central fact about Vulcans is that they are not naturally unemotional. They are a species of unusually violent passions who came close to destroying themselves in an era of savage warfare, and who were pulled back by a philosophical reform teaching the mastery of emotion through logic. Every serene Vulcan in the record is the product of lifelong training against a temperament that would otherwise be ungovernable. This distinction matters, and outsiders get it wrong constantly. Vulcans do not lack feeling; they decline to be governed by it. The discipline is a practice — meditation, rigorous self-examination, a vocabulary precise enough to describe an emotion without being carried by it — and like any practice it can lapse. A Vulcan under sufficient strain, injury, illness or chemical influence does not become mildly irritable; they become someone whose restraints have failed, and the setting treats that as genuinely dangerous. The tradition's ethical core is usually rendered as a principle of infinite diversity in infinite combinations: that the universe's variety is not an inconvenience to be tidied but the source of everything worth knowing. It is a striking doctrine to find at the centre of a culture famous for its severity, and it is the main reason Vulcans and the Federation fit together at all.

sections.heading: Society, Ritual and the Cycle
sections.body: Vulcan society is formal, hierarchical in matters of learning, and organised around clans and long obligation. Marriages are frequently arranged in childhood as a bond rather than a contract — a telepathic link that draws the pair together when it must be answered. That bond exists because Vulcan reproduction is periodic rather than continuous. At intervals an adult Vulcan enters a state in which the emotional controls fail completely, accompanied by a physiological crisis that is fatal if unresolved. It can be ended by returning to one's bonded partner, by ritual combat, or by extraordinary meditative discipline. The condition is the single most private matter in Vulcan life and is not discussed with outsiders, which makes its appearances in the record dramatic: a Vulcan is obliged to explain the one thing their culture forbids explaining, usually to save their own life. The setting uses the cycle to make a broader point about the civilisation. A society that has built its entire public identity on control is periodically and involuntarily reminded that the control is a construction over something older. Vulcan formality is not the absence of the savage past; it is the architecture holding it.

sections.heading: Vulcans and the Federation
sections.body: Vulcans were among the founding members of the Federation, and their early relationship with humans was difficult in ways the union has never entirely forgotten. Having made first contact with Earth, they spent decades as mentors who were also, in effect, restraints — convinced that humans were expanding faster than their judgement could support, and not always wrong. Human resentment of that period and Vulcan exasperation at human haste both survive into later eras as a familiar, almost familial friction. Within Starfleet, Vulcan officers are disproportionately represented in the sciences and are valued for exactly the qualities that make them uncomfortable company: they will state the unwelcome estimate, decline to soften a probability, and refuse to let a decision rest on how badly everyone wants it to work. The recurring pairing of a Vulcan officer with a human captain is the setting's most durable device for arguing with itself, because it puts the case for dispassion and the case for instinct in the same room and gives neither the final word. The Vulcans matter to this database because they are the setting's clearest study of a civilisation that made a deliberate, costly, collective choice about its own nature — and kept making it, every generation, because the alternative had nearly killed them.

guides.title: Klingons
guides.summary: A warrior culture written as a real civilisation: honour as law, the Empire's politics, and the long shift from adversary to ally.

sections.heading: Physiology and Temperament
sections.body: Klingons are physically formidable by human standards: stronger, more durable, and equipped with a redundancy of internal organs that lets them survive injuries that would kill most humanoids outright. The redundancy is thoroughgoing — duplicated major organs, a secondary circulatory arrangement — and it shapes their culture as much as their medicine, since a species that is genuinely hard to kill will develop different attitudes to risk. The most recognisable external feature is the ridged cranial structure, which varies considerably between individuals and family lines. The record contains a period during which many Klingons appeared without it, the result of a medical catastrophe involving genetic engineering and a viral agent; the affected generation regarded the loss as a disfigurement and the subject as unmentionable, which is the closest the Empire comes to open embarrassment. Temperamentally they are direct to a degree other species read as aggression and Klingons read as respect. Indirection is regarded as a form of contempt: to conceal your position from someone is to judge them unfit to hear it. Much of the friction between Klingons and Federation diplomats is not disagreement about substance but a mutual conviction that the other side is being insulting.

sections.heading: Honour as a Legal System
sections.body: Klingon honour is best understood not as a personal virtue but as the load-bearing structure of the society — closer to a constitution than to a sentiment. It determines inheritance, standing, the legitimacy of a command, and whether a family may hold a seat on the High Council. Its loss is not embarrassment; it is legal and economic ruin extending to one's descendants, which is why discommendation — formal expulsion from honourable society — functions in the setting as a punishment worse than execution. Because honour is structural, it is also political, and the Empire's most interesting stories are about the gap between the code and its use. Honour can be manufactured by a powerful house, withheld from a rival, or assigned to a lie that the Council finds convenient. A warrior may accept dishonour he did not earn because the alternative is a civil war the Empire cannot survive. The setting is unusually clear-eyed here: it presents a culture that genuinely believes its own code and is genuinely willing to corrupt it, and treats both as true at once. The code's better face is its treatment of death. A death in battle is not a misfortune but a completion, and a warrior's fear is not of dying but of dying without meaning. The associated rites — the roar that warns the dead that a warrior is coming, the vigil over the body, the insistence that the corpse is merely an empty shell once the spirit has gone — are among the most fully realised religious practices in the setting.

sections.heading: The Empire and Its Politics
sections.body: The Klingon Empire is governed by a High Council of great houses, presided over by a Chancellor. Power is held by families rather than parties, and the Council's business is largely the management of their rivalries. Succession is contested by challenge, and the legitimacy of a Chancellor rests on his ability to command the loyalty of enough houses to make deposing him expensive. This arrangement makes the Empire strong at the point of contact and structurally unstable behind it. An Empire whose leadership can be reorganised by a single successful challenge is one where an internal faction, a foreign power, or a well-placed impostor can achieve disproportionate effect — and the setting exploits that repeatedly, with outside powers engineering Klingon civil wars they could never have won directly. Religiously and culturally the Empire is organised around a founding figure who unified the warring houses, whose weapon is a relic of state, and whose promised return is a live political fact rather than a distant article of faith — as an episode involving a manufactured claimant demonstrates. The Empire's official position is that it killed its own gods, on the grounds that they were more trouble than they were worth: a joke that is also a fairly complete statement of the culture's attitude to authority.

sections.heading: From Adversary to Ally
sections.body: The Klingons enter the setting as the Federation's principal military rival, and the early period is one of open hostility punctuated by an imposed armistice. What makes the relationship durable as a piece of storytelling is that it does not stay there. The turn comes when the Empire suffers a catastrophe it cannot absorb alone — an environmental disaster of its own making — and faces the choice between accepting help from the power it despises and collapsing. The negotiation that follows is written as genuinely difficult: a peace made by two sides who have killed a great many of each other, brokered against factions on both sides who would rather fight, and paid for with the lives of some of the people who made it. The resulting accord converts the Klingons from enemy to uneasy ally over the following decades. The alliance never becomes comfortable, and the setting is better for it. Klingons in Starfleet are a standing anomaly — serving a power whose values they respect and whose caution they find contemptible — and the Empire remains capable of turning on the Federation when its own politics demand it. What the long arc establishes is the setting's most optimistic claim, made without sentimentality: that two civilisations organised around incompatible first principles can, at considerable cost and over generations, learn to hold a border together.

guides.title: Romulans
guides.summary: The Vulcans who refused the reform: an empire built on secrecy, suspicion and patience.

sections.heading: A Common Origin
sections.body: Romulans and Vulcans are the same species, separated by a schism rather than by evolution. When the philosophical reform that taught the mastery of emotion swept the Vulcan homeworld, a substantial faction rejected it, holding that passion was not a disease to be cured but the source of everything vital in them. Rather than submit, they left — a migration across interstellar distance undertaken with early technology, at enormous cost — and settled a new homeworld and its sister planet. The shared ancestry is the most important fact about them and, for a long period, an unknown one. The Federation fought a war with the Romulans without ever seeing their faces, and the revelation that its most implacable enemy was physically indistinguishable from its most respected ally arrived as a genuine shock, with immediate and ugly consequences for Vulcans serving in Starfleet. Physically the differences are slight and largely superficial: a brow ridge in many Romulan lines, a slighter build, and the loss over generations of the reliable touch-telepathy the Vulcan tradition cultivates. The important divergence is not biological. It is that one branch spent two millennia training itself out of its passions and the other spent the same two millennia building an empire with them intact.

sections.heading: The Star Empire
sections.body: The Romulan Star Empire is an authoritarian state built on secrecy. It is governed by a Senate under a Praetor, with real power distributed unevenly between the Senate, the military and — decisively — the Tal Shiar, the internal security service whose reach into every institution is the Empire's defining characteristic. A society in which the security service can arrest a fleet commander is one in which no one's loyalty is ever entirely settled, and Romulan behaviour follows from that permanent insecurity. Their strategic posture is patience. Where the Klingons are drawn as a power that strikes, the Romulans are drawn as a power that waits, prepares, and arranges for its opponents to weaken themselves. Their signature technology is the cloaking device, and it is a fair emblem of the whole civilisation: an enormous investment in not being seen until the moment of choosing. The Empire withdrew from interstellar affairs for decades at a stretch on more than one occasion, and those silences are treated as more alarming than its wars. A Romulan Empire that is not talking is a Romulan Empire that is doing something, and Federation intelligence assessments of the period read as extended exercises in anxious guesswork.

sections.heading: Character and Contradiction
sections.body: Romulans in the record are rarely simple. The recurring type is an officer of considerable personal honour serving a state that does not deserve it, aware of the gap and unwilling to act on that awareness — a characterisation the setting uses to make the Empire tragic rather than merely villainous. Their attitude to Vulcans is the sharpest thing about them: a mixture of contempt for a people who amputated their own passions and an unmistakable grief at the separation. The long underground movement for reunification, pursued by Romulans at mortal risk and encouraged by Vulcans with more hope than judgement, is one of the setting's most poignant threads precisely because both states have excellent reasons to suppress it. They are also, consistently, the most competent adversary the Federation faces. Klingon opposition can be met with force and Borg opposition with ingenuity, but Romulan opposition involves discovering that a situation the Federation thought it understood was arranged some years ago for a purpose it has not yet identified. Stories involving them tend to be about deduction rather than combat.

sections.heading: The Neutral Zone and After
sections.body: The Federation's border with the Empire is a demilitarised corridor established by treaty after their first war, entry into which by either side constitutes an act of war. It is one of the setting's most productive devices: a line that cannot be crossed, watched by two powers who each suspect the other of crossing it, generating decades of incidents in which the facts are genuinely unclear. The relationship never resolves into the Klingon pattern of eventual alliance. It produces instead a long series of partial thaws and sharp reversals — brief cooperation against a common threat, followed by a return to mutual surveillance. On the occasions the two powers do fight alongside one another, the collaboration is written as an alliance of arithmetic rather than of sentiment, and both sides expect it to end. In the later record the Empire suffers a catastrophe of the first order when its home system is destroyed by a stellar event, scattering the survivors and ending the Star Empire as it had existed. The aftermath — a proud, secretive, authoritarian civilisation reduced to dependence on the charity of a rival it spent centuries despising — gives the setting one of its most uncomfortable and most humane later subjects.

guides.title: Andorians
guides.summary: A cold-world people of martial honour and sensory antennae — and one of the Federation's founding members.

sections.heading: Biology and Homeworld
sections.body: Andorians are native to a frigid moon, and the adaptation shows in everything about them. Their skin carries a blue cast from a cobalt-based blood chemistry, their white hair reads as a cold-climate trait rather than as age, and they are visibly uncomfortable in the warm, humid conditions many other species find pleasant — a small detail that quietly explains why shared facilities in a mixed crew are always a compromise nobody is entirely happy with. The antennae are the feature that matters most and is most often misread as decoration. They are genuine sensory organs, sensitive to air movement, temperature gradients, electrical fields and sound, and they move — which means an Andorian's emotional state is legible to another Andorian at a distance and largely illegible to everyone else. Losing one is a serious injury rather than a cosmetic one; balance and spatial orientation both degrade. Andorian physiology is also notably robust. They tolerate injury and exertion that would incapacitate a human, and their metabolisms run hot enough that they require substantial food. A ship's physician treating a mixed crew has to hold several quite different baselines in mind at once, and Andorian norms sit at the far end of most of them.

sections.heading: A Culture of Formalised Aggression
sections.body: Andorian society is frequently described from outside as warlike, which is accurate but unhelpfully vague. What distinguishes it is not that Andorians fight but that fighting is heavily formalised. Disputes have procedures. Challenges have rules, seconds and accepted stopping points. The famous ritual duel is a legal instrument as much as a violent one, and the culture treats an unstructured brawl with far more contempt than a lethal duel conducted properly. This produces a people who read as hot-tempered and are in practice highly disciplined. An Andorian officer who is furious will usually say so plainly, which other species mistake for loss of control; the same officer will then follow the procedure exactly. The combination is why Andorians make effective military officers and difficult diplomats, and why the setting so often pairs them with species who mistake candour for hostility. Honour in the Andorian sense is closer to accountability than to reputation. An obligation incurred is tracked, and it is discharged. Debts of loyalty in particular are treated as binding well past the point where most cultures would consider them settled.

sections.heading: Family and the Question of Numbers
sections.body: Andorian reproduction is presented as involving more than two parties, with a bonded group rather than a couple as the basic family unit, and with the timing of that bonding constrained by biology rather than left to preference. The practical consequence is a culture in which marriage is arranged, scheduled and socially supervised, not because Andorians are unromantic but because delay carries a real cost. That cost is demographic. Andorian populations are portrayed as fragile — slow to grow, vulnerable to any disruption of the bonding structure, and acutely aware of it. A society that must actively work to sustain its own numbers behaves differently from one that does not: it is more conservative about its traditions, more suspicious of outside influence, and more inclined to read cultural change as an existential matter rather than a fashion. This is also where the setting locates most of its Andorian drama. A young Andorian resisting an arranged bonding is not simply chafing at an old custom; they are weighing personal freedom against a collective survival argument that is not obviously wrong.

sections.heading: Andorians in the Federation
sections.body: Andoria is one of the founding worlds, and the founding is the more remarkable for how badly Andorians and Vulcans got on beforehand. The two were rivals for generations, with Andorians regarding Vulcan logic as sanctimonious cover for manipulation and Vulcans regarding Andorian candour as barely governed violence. Both readings contained enough truth to keep the hostility alive. What ended it was a shared problem neither could solve alone, brokered by a third party with no stake in the old grievance. That pattern — enemies who become allies because the alternative is worse, and who then discover the alliance was the better arrangement anyway — is the Federation's founding story in miniature, and Andorians are its clearest illustration. In Starfleet, Andorians are disproportionately represented in the tactical and security branches, which is exactly the stereotype and is also true. The more interesting Andorian officers in the setting are the ones who took a different path deliberately, and who have to keep explaining themselves to their own people rather than to anyone else.

guides.title: Tellarites
guides.summary: The founding member nobody quotes: why a culture that argues constantly is easy to underestimate.

sections.heading: A People Built on Argument
sections.body: Tellarites are the fourth founding species and the one least often described accurately. They are short, stocky, tusked and abrasive, and every summary stops there. What actually defines the culture is that argument is the normal register of respectful conversation. A Tellarite who insults your reasoning is engaging with it. A Tellarite who is polite to you has concluded that you are not worth the effort. This inverts the assumption almost every other species brings to a negotiating table, and the resulting misunderstandings are entirely predictable: humans read Tellarite debate as personal attack, Vulcans read it as emotional incontinence, and Tellarites read everyone else's smoothing-over as evasion. The practical upshot is that Tellarites are excellent at finding the weakness in a proposal and poor at making anyone want to hear it. A mixed committee containing a Tellarite produces better decisions and takes longer to reach them, which is a trade the Federation appears to have made knowingly.

sections.heading: Engineering, Trade and Craft
sections.body: Tellarite prominence in engineering and shipbuilding follows directly from the argumentative temperament. A culture where every design is attacked on sight by colleagues who consider attacking it a courtesy produces robust designs, because the weak ones do not survive the first review. Tellarite yards have a reputation for building things that work and for taking longer than promised to agree on what to build. They are also traders, and the same instincts apply. Tellarite commerce assumes haggling as the default rather than the exception, and a fixed price is received as either an insult or an admission that the seller does not understand their own goods. A merchant from a fixed-price culture will find a Tellarite counterpart exhausting and will usually end up with a better deal than they expected, having been talked into defending a number they had not previously examined. The stereotype of Tellarite stubbornness is real but mis-sited. They will change position readily when the argument against them is good. What they will not do is change position to end an uncomfortable conversation.

sections.heading: Why the Federation Needed Them
sections.body: The founding coalition is usually told as a Vulcan-human story with Andorians as the complication. Tellarites are the reason the resulting institution has procedure at all. A federation of species that all valued harmony would have produced consensus documents nobody could enforce. Tellarite participation forced the founders to write things down precisely, to define terms, and to build appeal mechanisms — because a Tellarite delegation will find every ambiguity in a charter and will do so publicly. The Federation's habit of exhaustive regulation, so often played for comedy, has a Tellarite fingerprint on it. The same contribution shows in the Federation's treatment of dissent. An institution shaped in part by a species that regards objection as participation is unlikely to treat objection as disloyalty, and the setting's Federation is notably tolerant of officers who argue with their superiors, provided they do it before the order is given rather than after.

sections.heading: Tellarites Aboard Ship
sections.body: A Tellarite in a Starfleet crew is a specific kind of colleague. They will tell a captain that a plan is bad in front of the bridge crew, without lowering their voice, and will implement it without complaint once the decision is made. The first behaviour reads as insubordination to anyone unfamiliar; the second is what proves it was not. Officers who work well with Tellarites tend to be the ones who learn to argue back. Deference gets nowhere — a Tellarite hearing agreement assumes the other party has not thought about it. The productive response to a Tellarite objection is a better counter-argument, delivered with equal force, after which the matter is usually settled and neither party regards it as having been a quarrel. This makes Tellarites a useful test of an institution's health. Where they are valued, the organisation is genuinely open to being told it is wrong. Where they are quietly excluded from rooms, something has gone wrong that nobody has yet said aloud.

guides.title: Ferengi
guides.summary: A civilisation organised entirely around profit — used by the setting as a mirror rather than a joke.

sections.heading: Commerce as a Total System
sections.body: Ferengi society treats acquisition the way other cultures treat religion, law and family combined. Profit is not merely permitted; it is the organising principle from which obligation, status and even the afterlife are derived.
